newsitem.title: USA: Top U.S. margarine maker settles deceptive ad charges.
newsitem.headline: Top U.S. margarine maker settles deceptive ad charges.

text.p: The nation's largest margarine maker signed an agreement with the Federal Trade Commission to settle charges of deceptive advertising that Promise margarine helps to prevent heart disease, the FTC announced Thursday.

The agreement was with Conopco Inc. and Van den Bergh Foods Co., subsidiaries of the giant international food company Unilever. Van den Bergh, based in Lisle, Ill., is the biggest manufacturer of margarine in the United States and produces the Promise margarine line and other major margarine brands.

The FTC had charged that Promise margarine's "Get Heart Smart" campaign -- which claimed the margarine would help reduce the risk of heart disease because of its low content of total and unsaturated fat -- was unsubstantiated, false and deceptive.
The FTC targeted the campaigns of the Promise margarine spread, Promise Extra Light margarine and Promise Ultra spread. It did not challenge claims for Promise Ultra Fat Free Nonfat spread.

The margarine market in the United States is huge. Last year, Americans consumed more than 2.4 billion pounds of margarine, equal to almost 10 pounds per person. Butter consumption trailed at 1.2 billion pounds, or about 5 pounds per person.
In television commercials and print ads for Promise margarine that FTC said ran until July 1995, newspaper headlines were shown which said heart disease is the nation's No. 1 killer.

Heart-shaped pats of margarine on food items such as pancakes were then featured, along with a package of Promise spread with the statements "Low in Saturated Fat" and "No Cholesterol." The commercials concluded with the "Get Heart Smart" slogan.
"The evidence was not adequate to suppport the absolute and unqualified heart disease claim," said the FTC in a release announcing the settlement. "And the fat-content claims are false."

Margarine is made from polyunsaturated fat and is hardened liquid vegetable oil. Promise margarine spread, which contains 9.5 grams of fat per tablespoon, has nearly the same fat content as a stick of butter which has 10 to 14 grams of fat per tablespoon.
Under the agreement, the makers of Promise have agreed to refrain from making any health claim unless it has "adequate scientific substantiation."

The agreement also prohibits the firm from misrepresenting the amount of fat, staturated fat, cholesterol or calories in any spread or margarine, and required the firm to follow the labeling regulations of the Food and Drug Administration when making any nutrient claim or cholesterol claim.

"This was an amicable solution," said John Gould, spokesman for Van den Bergh Foods. Gould said the company's advertising strategy for Promise has changed, and that, "we're dealing with another chapter now."
